replacement: 8. You see, these philosophers are far from being uncorrupted witnesses or judges of what the ascetic ideal is worth. They are thinking of themselves — what is the "saint" to them? What they have in mind is whatever they personally cannot do without: release from compulsion, disturbance and noise; release from business, duties and cares; a clear head; thoughts that dance, spring and fly; and good air — rare, clear, free and dry, the air of the heights, in which every animal creature grows more intellectual and sprouts wings. They have in mind peace in every cellar; every hound neatly chained; no baying of enmity, no uncouth rancor; no remorse from wounded ambition; internal organs that are quiet and submissive, busy as mills yet unnoticed; a heart that is alien, transcendent, future, posthumous. In short, what they mean by the ascetic ideal is the joyous asceticism of an animal that has been deified and newly fledged, and that sweeps over life instead of resting on it. The three great catch-words of the ascetic ideal are familiar to us: poverty, humility, chastity. Now look closely at the lives of all the great, fruitful, inventive spirits. Again and again you will find these three qualities in them, to a certain degree. This is, of course, not for a minute as though, perhaps, they belonged among such men's virtues — what has this type of man to do with virtues? — but because they are the most essential and natural conditions of such a man's best existence and finest fruitfulness. It is quite possible, in this connection, that their dominant intellectualism first had to rein in an unruly, irritable pride, or an insolent sensualism, or that it had its work cut out defending its wish for the "desert" against perhaps a leaning toward luxury and dilettantism, or against an extravagant generosity of heart and hand. Their intellect managed all this for one simple reason: it was the dominant instinct, and it imposed its orders on all the other instincts. It still does so; if it ceased, it would no longer be dominant. But in all this there is not one iota of "virtue." Further, take the desert I just mentioned, where the strong, independent and well-equipped spirits withdraw into their hermitage — oh, how unlike the desert the cultured classes dream of! In certain cases the cultured classes themselves are the desert. And it is certain that none of the actors of the intellect could endure that desert for even a minute. It is not romantic or Syrian enough for them; it is nowhere near enough of a stage desert! There are plenty of asses here too, but the resemblance stops there. A desert today looks more like this — perhaps a deliberate obscurity; stepping out of one's own way; a dread of noise, admiration, newspapers, influence; a little office, a daily task, something that conceals rather than reveals; at times the company of harmless, cheerful beasts and fowls whose sight refreshes; a mountain for company, though not a dead one, one with eyes (that is, with lakes); in some cases even a room in a crowded hotel, where one can count on going unrecognized and on talking with anyone without risk. That is the desert — oh, it is lonely enough, believe me! I admit that when Heracleitus withdrew to the courts and cloisters of the colossal temple of Artemis, his "wilderness" was worthier. Why do we lack such temples? (Perhaps we do not; I am thinking just now of my splendid study in the Piazza di San Marco, in spring, of course, and in the morning, between ten and twelve.) But what Heracleitus fled, we too avoid today: the noise and democratic babble of the Ephesians, their politics, their news from the "empire" (Persia, I mean, of course), their market-trade in "the things of today." For there is one thing above all that we philosophers need a rest from: the things of "today." We honor whatever is silent, cold, noble, far and past — in fact, anything the sight of which does not force the soul to brace and defend itself; something one can speak with without speaking aloud. Now listen to the tone of a spirit when it speaks; every spirit has a tone of its own and loves it. That one over there, for instance, is bound to be an agitator, that is, a hollow head, a hollow mug: whatever goes in comes back out of him dull and thick, heavy with the echo of the great void. That other spirit nearly always speaks hoarsely. Has he, perhaps, thought himself hoarse? It may be so — ask the physiologists. But someone who thinks in words thinks as a speaker and not as a thinker (this shows that he does not think about objects, or think objectively, but only about his relations to objects; in fact, that he thinks only of himself and his audience). A third speaks aggressively; he comes too near our body and his breath blows on us — we involuntarily shut our mouths, though he speaks to us through a book. The tone of his style supplies the reason: he has no time, he has little faith in himself, he finds expression now or never. A spirit who is sure of himself, however, speaks softly; he seeks secrecy and lets himself be waited for. A philosopher is recognized by his shunning three brilliant and noisy things, fame, princes and women — which is not to say that they do not come to him. He shuns every glaring light, and so he shuns his own time and its "daylight." In this he is like a shadow: the lower the sun sinks, the larger the shadow grows. As for his humility, he puts up with a certain dependence and obscurity just as he puts up with darkness. Further, he is afraid of the shock of lightning; he shudders at the insecurity of a tree that stands too isolated and exposed, on which every storm vents its temper and every temper its storm. His "maternal" instinct, his secret love for what is growing in him, leads him into states in which he is relieved of the need to look after himself, just as the "mother" instinct in woman has thoroughly preserved her dependent position down to the present. After all, they ask little enough, these philosophers; their favorite motto is, "He who possesses is possessed." As I must say again and again, none of this is to be put down to a virtue or to a meritorious wish for moderation and simplicity. It happens because their supreme lord demands it of them, wisely and inexorably — a lord who is eager for one thing only, and for that alone gathers and hoards everything: time, strength, love, interest. This kind of man does not like being disturbed by enmity, nor by friendship; it is a type that forgets or despises easily. He finds it bad form to play the martyr, to "suffer for truth"; he leaves that to the ambitious and the stage-heroes of the intellect, and to all those who have time for such luxuries (the philosophers themselves have something to do for truth). They use big words sparingly; they are said to dislike the very word "truth," which has a "high falutin'" ring. Finally, as for the chastity of philosophers: the fruitfulness of this type of mind lies plainly in another sphere than children; perhaps it is in some other sphere, too, that they have the survival of their name, their little immortality (philosophers in ancient India would say it with still greater boldness: "Of what use is posterity to him whose soul is the world?"). In this attitude there is no trace of chastity out of any ascetic scruple or hatred of the flesh, any more than it is chastity when an athlete or a jockey stays away from women. It is rather the will of the dominant instinct, at any rate during the time of their advanced philosophic pregnancy. Every artist knows how harmful sexual intercourse is in times of great mental strain and preparation. For the strongest artists, those with the surest instincts, this is not necessarily a matter of experience — hard experience; it is simply their "maternal" instinct, which, for the benefit of the growing work, recklessly spends the vigor of its animal life (beyond all its normal stocks and supplies). The greater power then absorbs the lesser. Now let us use this interpretation to judge correctly the case of Schopenhauer, already mentioned. In his case the sight of the beautiful evidently worked like a resolving irritant on the chief power of his nature (the power of contemplation and intense penetration), so that this strength exploded and suddenly became master of his consciousness. But that does not at all rule out the possibility that the particular sweetness and fullness peculiar to the æsthetic state springs directly from an ingredient of sensuality (just as the "idealism" peculiar to girls at puberty has the same source). It may be, then, that sensuality is not removed when the æsthetic state approaches, as Schopenhauer believed, but only transfigured, so that it no longer enters consciousness as sexual excitement. (I shall come back to this point in connection with the more delicate problems of the physiology of the æsthetic, a subject that has so far been singularly untouched and unelucidated.)
